summary: This informational document discusses how to evaluate Information-Centric Networking and what its effects on network security might be. It surveys the tools currently available to researchers working on ICN and offers suggestions about methodology and metrics.

plainLanguage.summary: This document helps researchers test Information-Centric Networking, a design where the network delivers named information instead of connecting two hosts. It says what to fix when running an experiment, which numbers to record, and where the security holes are.

subtitle: Testing and securing a name-based networking approach

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking proposals are published with results that cannot be compared, because each study uses its own topology, traffic and metrics, and the security side of the idea has barely been examined.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out what to fix when running an ICN experiment, which metrics to record, and where the security and privacy gaps lie in the proposed architectures.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance for researchers rather than a specification: it gives a common reference point for experiments and a list of security issues that still need solving before ICN could be deployed.

today: RFC 7945 is an Informational document from the IRTF with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it remains the ICNRG's guidance on how to evaluate information-centric networking and where its security gaps are. It is explicitly not a standard, and it notes that the research field is still young, with trace-based analysis of ICN in its infancy.

sections.title: What ICN Is and Why It Is Hard to Evaluate
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking is a networking concept that arose from the desire to align the operation model of a network with the model of its typical use. For TCP/IP networks this implies changing the mechanisms of data access and transport from a host-to-host model to a user-to-information model. The premise is that the effort invested in changing models will be offset, or even surpassed, by the potential of a better network, but such a claim can be validated only if it is quantified.

Different ICN approaches are evaluated in the peer-reviewed literature using a mixture of theoretical analysis, simulation and emulation techniques, and empirical testbed measurements. The specific methodology depends on the goal, whether one wants to evaluate scalability, quantify resource utilization or analyse economic incentives. Ease and convenience of setting up and running experiments can also be a factor in published evaluations. As discussed in RFC 7476, the development phase ICN is going through and the plethora of approaches to tackle the hardest problems make this a very active and growing research area, but that also makes it more difficult to compare different proposals on an equal footing.

Performance evaluation using real network deployments has the advantage of realistic workloads, but in the case of ICN it is not clear what qualifies as a realistic workload. Trace-based analysis of ICN is in its infancy and more work is needed towards defining characteristic workloads for ICN evaluation studies. Numerous factors affect experimental results: the topology selected, the background traffic an application is subjected to, network conditions such as available link capacities, link delays and loss-rate characteristics throughout the topology, failure and disruption patterns, node mobility, and the diversity of devices used.

The document's goal is to summarise evaluation guidelines and tools alongside suggested data sets and high-level approaches, so that researchers and practitioners can compare and contrast different ICN designs as well as the state of the art in host-centric solutions and identify their respective strengths and weaknesses. It notes that apart from the technical evaluation of an ICN architecture's functionality, the future success of ICN will be largely driven by its deployability and economic viability, so evaluations should assess incremental deployability in the existing network environment together with a view of how the technical functions will incentivise deployers to invest in the capabilities that allow the architecture to spread.

The document is a product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group, whose main objective is to couple ongoing ICN research with solutions relevant for evolving the Internet at large, and whose documents provide guidelines for experimental activities so that different alternative solutions can be compared consistently. It does not constitute an IETF standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is that the network should deliver named information rather than connect two computers. That is hard to measure fairly, because every research paper picks its own test network, its own traffic and its own numbers. This document tries to put a common set of choices in place.

sections.title: Setting Up the Experiment: Topology and Traffic
sections.content:
The way IP networks are evaluated does not apply directly to ICN. In IP the focus is on the performance and characteristics of end-to-end connections between a source and a destination. In ICN the source responding to a request can be any node in the network and may change from request to request, which makes it difficult to use concepts like delay and throughput in a traditional way. Evaluating resource usage is also more complicated, since memory used for caching affects delays and the use of transmission resources.

On topology, the classic dumbbell topology used for host-centric work is regarded as inappropriate for ICN, and most ICN studies have used it anyway. There is no single topology that can easily evaluate all aspects of ICN, so one should choose from a range depending on the focus. For scalability and resilience studies there is a wide range of synthetic topologies, such as the Barabasi-Albert model and the Watts-Strogatz small-world topology, which allow experiments while controlling key parameters such as node degree; these are appropriate in general because there are no practical assurances that a future information-centric network will have the same topology as today's networks. When studies look at cost or migration to ICN, realistic topologies should be used, inferred from Internet traces such as the CAIDA Macroscopic Internet Topology Data Kit and Rocketfuel, with the problem that the size of such a topology, approximately 45K Autonomous Systems and close to 200K links, may limit the scalability of the evaluation tool. Studies focusing on node or content mobility can benefit from the topologies and dynamic aspects used in the Delay-Tolerant Networking community, where DTN traces are available.

As with host-centric topologies, defining just a node graph is not enough: the experimenter should also define the network, storage and computation capacities available at each node and the delay characteristics of each link. On traffic load, the document offers a content catalog for different scenarios, based on previously published work, usable to evaluate proposals on routing, congestion control and performance. Since ICN-specific traffic workloads are still lacking, today's workloads can only be extrapolated from. A significant challenge is identifying the applications contributing to the observed traffic and the exact amount each contributes.

The document points to today's mix of Web, peer-to-peer file sharing and User-Generated Content platforms such as YouTube, and Video on Demand services, with publicly available traces. It cites a large-scale measurement study in which Web traffic amounted to 52% of all measured traffic, while deep packet inspection revealed that 25-40% of all HTTP traffic actually carries video. Deep packet inspection also showed the difficulty of correctly identifying the application type for peer-to-peer traffic: mapping observed port numbers to well-known applications puts P2P at only 0.85% of overall traffic, while deep packet inspection raises that to 18.32%, and a study on a large ISP put P2P between 17% and 19% of overall traffic. The catalog for each type of traffic is characterised by the cardinality of the estimated content catalog, the size of the exchanged contents, either chunks or entire named information objects, and the popularity of objects expressed as their request frequency.

In most application types the popularity distribution follows a power law, indicating that a small number of information items trigger a large proportion of the whole set of requests, and the exact shape of that distribution directly affects protocol performance: highly skewed distributions favour caching, since caching a very small set of items can dramatically increase the cache hit ratio. Zipf's law is the discrete distribution that best represents request frequency in a number of application scenarios, ranging from the Web to Video on Demand, where the frequency of a request is inversely proportional to the rank of the content. The popularity of a Zipf distribution is given by P(X=i) = (1 / i^(alpha)) / C, with C = SUM(1 / j^(alpha)) and alpha greater than zero. A later analysis of HTTP traffic found content popularity better reflected by a trimodal model in which the head and tail of a Zipf distribution with slope 0.84 are replaced by two discrete Weibull distributions with shape parameters 0.5 and 0.24. A variation called the Mandelbrot-Zipf distribution was suggested for environments where nodes can locally store previously requested content, since peer-to-peer file sharing applications typically exhibit a fetch-at-most-once behaviour because peers tend to persist the files they download, a behaviour that may also be prevalent in ICN.
sections.plainLanguage: To compare two ICN designs fairly, both must run on the same test network and the same traffic. The document recommends standard topologies for scalability work, real Internet maps for cost work, and a common catalog of content sizes and popularities, because a few very popular items drive most of the traffic and that shapes how well caching works.

sections.title: Choosing Metrics That Mean Something
sections.content:
Quantifying network performance requires a set of standard metrics. They should be broad enough to apply equally to host-centric and information-centric networks, so that an ICN approach can be compared with an earlier version of itself, with another ICN approach, or with the incumbent host-centric approach. At the same time they should target network performance only and avoid expanding into the physical and application layers, and at this point it is more important to capture the main figures of merit and leave the more esoteric and less frequent cases for the future.

Looking at the metrics used in existing approaches such as CCN, NetInf, PURSUIT, COMET, Connect and CONVERGENCE, they fall into two categories: metrics for the approach as a whole, and metrics for individual components such as name resolution and routing. Metrics for the whole approach are further split into traffic and system metrics. The approaches do not name or define metrics consistently, which is a major problem when trying to compare them, so the document classifies similarly defined metrics under the same name and reports only the most common ones. Throughput and download time seem to be the most popular metrics altogether. The most common system metrics are protocol overhead, total traffic, transit traffic, cost savings, router cost and router energy consumption. Among component metrics, Forwarding Information Base size and path length are almost ubiquitous, perhaps because of the networking background of the researchers involved.

For traffic metrics, the document considers three places to measure. At the output of the network, using IP Performance Metrics such as delay, delay variation, loss, reordering and duplication, work that the IETF has done for more than a decade under the framework of RFC 2330. Because those metrics and methods already work for host-centric networks, comparing them with information-centric networks would entail only the ICN extension of the framework, and measuring transport performance at the output can be done mostly without any dependence on applications, although more study is needed to turn the claim into a certainty. At the input to the application, quality-of-service metrics such as startup latency, playout lag and playout continuity for a live video-streaming application abstract away the details of the underlying transport network and can be applied to networks of different concepts, but they depend on the application, so different types of application will require different metrics. At the output of the application, quality-of-experience metrics measure what the user perceives; the standardized method for obtaining a Mean Opinion Score for VoIP is quite different from that for IPTV, and such methods are notoriously hard to implement because they involve real users in a controlled environment, or are intrusive if they model human perception instead. The most important drawback is that only part of such a measurement relates to network performance, with the rest relating to application performance such as video coding or device capabilities, which are generally hard to separate. The document therefore sees quality-of-experience metrics as a poor choice at this stage.

For system metrics, the document lists reliability, scalability, energy efficiency and delay or disconnection tolerance. In constrained environments, processing requirements, signalling overhead and memory allocation for caching procedures matter, as do power consumption and battery lifetime. For gateways, which act as a point of service to many nodes, scalability metrics such as the frequency and processing of successfully satisfied information requests matter. Because ICNs cache in the network, efficiency and performance metrics for in-network caching have to be defined, and a first step is a formula that approximates the proportion of time a piece of content stays in a network cache, taking as input the request rate for that content, the rate of requests for all other contents that move it down the cache, and the size of the cache in slots. Written as pi = [mu / (mu + lambda)]^N, where lambda is the request rate for the content of interest, mu the rate of requests for contents that move it down the cache and N the cache size, the model reflects the probability that the content will be found in a given cache.
sections.plainLanguage: Which numbers to record is itself a choice. Measuring delay and loss at the edge of the network keeps the application out of the picture, which is what the document prefers. Measuring how good the picture looks to a person is hard to do and mostly measures the application rather than the network.

sections.title: ICN Security Aspects
sections.content:
The introduction of an information-centric networking architecture and the corresponding communication paradigm results in changes to many aspects of network security, affecting all the scenarios described in RFC 7476. The aspects described reflect the ICN security challenges outlined in RFC 7927. The architectures currently proposed have concentrated on authentication of delivered content to ensure its integrity, and although those approaches are primarily applicable to freely accessible content that does not require access authorisation, they will generally support delivery of encrypted content. The introduction of widespread caching mechanisms may also provide additional attack surfaces. In practice the work on security in the various ICN research projects has been heavily concentrated on authentication of content; work on authorisation, access control, privacy and security threats due to the expanded role of in-network caches has been quite limited. As secure communications on the Internet become the norm, major gaps in ICN security aspects are bound to undermine adoption.

Authentication. For fully secure content distribution, the receiver must be able to assess validity, meaning whether it is a complete, uncorrupted copy of what was originally published; provenance, meaning whether the receiver can identify the publisher and whether the source of any cached version can be trusted; and relevance, meaning whether the content answers the question that was asked. All the architectures considered target the validity requirement using strong cryptographic means to tie the content request name to the content. Provenance and relevance are targeted to varying extents, in a trade-off between the simplicity and efficiency of access and the level of assurance: maintaining provenance information can become extremely costly, particularly when considering historic relationships between multiple objects, so each architecture has decided whether the assessment is carried out by the network or left to the application. An additional consideration is whether a name should be irrevocably tied to static, pre-existing content or whether it can refer to dynamically generated content. Schemes that only target immutable content can be less resource-hungry, using digest functions rather than public key cryptography for generating and checking signatures, but this can increase the load on applications because they must manage many names rather than use a single name for an item of evolving content.

Authorisation, access control and logging. A potentially major concern for all the architectures considered is that they provide no inbuilt support for an authorisation framework or for logging. Once content has been published and cached in servers, routers or endpoints not controlled by the publisher, the publisher has no way to enforce access control, determine which users have accessed the content, or revoke its publication; in some cases, where requests do not necessarily carry host or user identifier information, it is difficult for publishers themselves to perform access control. Access could be limited by encrypting the content, but the necessity of distributing keys out of band appears to negate the advantages of in-network caching and creates significant challenges when managing and restricting key access. An authorisation delegation scheme has been proposed that allows semi-trusted entities such as caches or CDN nodes to delegate access control decisions to third-party access control providers trusted by the content publisher; the former entities have no access to subscriber-related information and should respect the decisions of the providers. Another proposal gives control of the name resolution infrastructure to the publisher, which enables access logging and some degree of active cache management, such as purging of stale content. Attribute-Based Encryption is a possible technique for providing access control to heterogeneous groups while still allowing a single encrypted object representation that remains cacheable. Evaluating the impact of the absence of these features will be essential for any scenario where ICN might be deployed, and may have a seriously negative impact on its applicability in commercial environments unless a solution can be found.

Privacy. This is another area the architectures have not significantly analysed. Caching implies a trade-off between network efficiency and privacy, and the activity of users is significantly more exposed to the scrutiny of cache owners with whom they may have no relationship. It should be noted that only the first-hop router or cache can see who requests what, as requests are aggregated and only the previous-hop router is visible when a request is forwarded. Although in many architectures the source of a request is not explicitly identified, an attacker monitoring transactions on the cache may obtain considerable information: details of the objects accessed, the topological direction of requests and information about the timing of transactions. The persistence of data in the cache makes life easier for an attacker by giving a longer timescale for analysis.

Changes to the threat model. The architectural differences of the ICN models have consequences for network security, and there is limited consideration of threat models and mitigations in the documents describing the architectures. The key aspects the document lists are that caching implies the trade-off between network efficiency and user privacy; that more powerful routers upgraded to handle persistent caching increase the network's attack surface, particularly in systems that perform cryptographic checks on cached content, since not doing so could lead routers to disseminate invalid content; that ICN makes it difficult to identify the origin of a request, slowing the process of blocking requests and requiring alternative mechanisms to differentiate legitimate from inappropriate ones, as access control lists will probably be of little value for ICN requests; that denial-of-service attacks may require more effort on ICN but are still feasible, because it is difficult to force repeated requests for the same content onto a single node, since ICNs naturally spread content, though there are many ways around this, such as generating random suffix identifiers that always result in cache misses; and that per-request state in routers can be abused for denial-of-service attacks. Caches can be misused in three further ways: attackers can use caches as storage to make their own content available, the efficiency of caches can be decreased with the goal of a denial-of-service attack, and content can be extracted by any attacker connected to the cache, putting users' privacy at risk.
sections.plainLanguage: The security work on these architectures has mostly been about checking that content is not corrupted. The document says the gaps are elsewhere: there is no way for a publisher to control who reads what once copies are cached in routers, caching exposes what users ask for, and requests cannot easily be traced back to a person, so blocking them is harder.

sections.title: The Tools Researchers Use
sections.content:
Since ICN is an emerging area, the community is developing evaluation environments: open-source implementations, simulators, emulators and testbeds. To date none of the available tools can be seen as the one and only community reference evaluation tool, and no single environment supports all well-known ICN approaches, which hinders direct comparison of results.

Among the open-source implementations, the Named Data Networking project has open-sourced a software reference implementation called NDN, available for deployment on various operating systems, with C and Java libraries for building applications. CCN-lite is a lightweight implementation of the CCN protocol that supports most key features of CCNx and is interoperable with it, implementing the core CCN logic in about 1000 lines of code, which makes it ideal for classroom work and for quickly experimenting with CCN extensions. PARC offers CCN source code under various licensing schemes. The PURSUIT project has open-sourced its Blackhawk publish-subscribe implementation for Linux and Android, built on the Click modular router, and the POINT project maintains Blackadder. The 4WARD and SAIL projects have open-sourced software implementing different aspects of NetInf, including the NetInf URI format and HTTP and UDP convergence layer; the Java implementation provides a local caching proxy and client, and an OpenNetInf prototype is available as well as a hybrid host-centric and information-centric architecture called the Global Information Network, with a browser plug-in and video-streaming software.

Simulators and emulators should capture faithfully all features and operations of the architectures they model, with any limitations openly documented, and must come with adequate logging facilities for in-depth analysis and debugging. Other requirements include supporting medium- to large-scale experiments, quickly and correctly setting configurations and parameters, and playing back traffic traces captured on a real testbed or network. This does not begin to address the need for strong validation of any evaluated implementation.

ndnSIM is a module that plugs into the ns-3 simulator and supports the core features of NDN, usable to experiment with NDN applications and services as well as components such as routing protocols and caching and forwarding strategies. ccnSIM is a CCN-specific simulator designed to handle forwarding of a large number of CCN chunks, written in C++ for the OMNeT++ framework; other CCN-specific simulators include the CCN Packet-Level Simulator and CCN-Joker, which emulates in user space all basic aspects of a CCN node, including handling of Interest and Data packets, cache sizing and replacement policies, and both flow and congestion control. The Icarus simulator focuses on caching in ICN and is agnostic with respect to any particular ICN implementation; it is written in Python, uses the Fast Network Simulator Setup tool, and has several caching strategies including ProbCache, which takes a resource management view of caching decisions and approximates the available cache capacity along the path so that it caches content probabilistically to reduce redundancy; node-centrality-based caching, where the node with the highest betweenness centrality along the path is responsible for caching incoming content; and hash-route-based caching, which computes the hash of a content's name and assigns contents to caches of a domain accordingly, an off-path strategy that requires minimum coordination and redirection overhead. Icarus also includes the Satisfied Interest Table, which points in the direction where content has been sent recently and enables information resilience when the network fragments.

On experimental facilities, the document notes that with the disruptive nature of clean-slate approaches generating new technological requirements, it is complex to provide meaningful results for a network-layer framework compared with what is deployed in the current Internet, so the need for large-scale environments supporting experimental evaluation is of prime importance. Facilities differ in characteristics such as low cost of use, reproducible configuration, easy-to-use tools, available background traffic, and being sharable. The Open Network Lab supports CCN and comprises 18 extensible gigabit routers and over a 100 computers representing clients, freely available to the public, with nodes preloaded with CCNx software and a graphical user interface for configuration that also serves as a control mechanism. CCN can also be run over testbeds such as PlanetLab, Emulab, DeterLab and OFELIA by directly running the open-source code, and the Network Experimentation Programming Interface is a tool for controlling and managing large-scale experiments. The POINT testbed has 40 machines across Europe, North America at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Japan at the National Institute of Information and Communications Technology, interconnected in a topology with one Topology Manager and one rendezvous node handling all publish-subscribe and topology formation requests; all machines run Blackadder, new nodes can join, and experiments can be run on request. CUTEi is a testbed from NICT comprising multiple servers in Asia and other locations, each using a Linux kernel-based container for node virtualisation, with two experimentation modes using two container designs: application-level experimentation using a common container shared by all users, and network-level experimentation using a user container assigned to one user, which has a private IP address and a user space providing a closed networking environment. The testbed also implements an on-filesystem cache with an individual cache accessible to one dedicated router and a shared cache accessible to a set of routers in the same group, to avoid duplicated caching in the neighbourhood.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no single ICN test environment. The document lists what exists: open-source code for the main architectures, simulators that plug into larger tools, and three physical testbeds ranging from eighteen routers to forty machines spread across three countries. That variety is exactly the problem the document is trying to solve.

sections.title: Security Considerations of This Document
sections.content: The document states that it does not impact the security of the Internet, but that Section 3 outlines security and privacy concerns that might affect a deployment of a future ICN approach. It is a research report: the security material it discusses concerns the architectures it surveys rather than any mechanism the document itself defines.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds nothing to Internet security itself, since it defines no protocol. Its security discussion is about the risks in the architectures it reviews.

items.title: Caching and privacy
items.text: Users' activity is exposed to cache owners they have no relationship with.

items.title: Bigger attack surface
items.text: Routers upgraded to cache persistently, and to check content cryptographically, gain new ways to be attacked.

items.title: Hard to trace a request
items.text: The origin of a request is difficult to identify, so blocking it is slower and access control lists are of little value.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: Still feasible, but harder, since content spreads across the network. Random name suffixes can defeat caching and force the origin to serve.

items.title: Caches can be abused
items.text: Attackers can store their own content in a cache, fill it to slow others down, or extract content from it.
